korTTY can be built as Java artifacts, a self-contained portable application image or a native installer. Native packages must be built on the target operating system and processor architecture because KTPH000, JavaFX and the bundled native tools select platform-specific files from the active build machine.
Yes, plus every runtime dependency; this JAR is not a stand-alone executable JAR
Yes; the archive includes dependencies and launch scripts but no Java runtime
Platform app bundle or directory under KTPH000
No; KTPH000 includes a trimmed Java runtime
DMG, MSI, DEB or RPM under KTPH000
No; the installer contains the self-contained app image
KTPH000, then the OS archive command shown below
ZIP or TAR containing the entire app image
No; keep the bundle or directory intact after extraction
An app image is not one executable file

On macOS the app image is the complete KTPH000 bundle, on Windows it is the complete KTPH001 directory containing KTPH002, and on Linux it is the complete KTPH003 directory containing KTPH004. Moving only the launcher breaks the application because its runtime and libraries remain in sibling directories. The Linux directory is not a KTPH005 file.
Install these tools before building on any operating system:
A full JDK supported by the pinned Gradle wrapper
Starts Gradle; korTTY then resolves a matching Temurin JDK 25 toolchain for compilation, KTPH000 and KTPH001
Clones korTTY and the pinned SithTermFX source dependency
Builds SithTermFX into the local Maven repository before korTTY compilation
Downloads the pinned mosh4j artifacts used by packaged builds
The wrapper, Maven/Gradle dependencies, SithTermFX, SHA-256-pinned mosh4j, the Monaco build toolchain, formatter browser bundles and chat-render resources are downloaded during a clean first build
KTPH000 and KTPH001 download and run the repository-pinned Gradle version; do not install or substitute a system Gradle

Node.js and MkDocs are not common prerequisites for an application build: Gradle downloads a pinned Node.js runtime into an isolated build directory only to compile Monaco, never into the application image, and the normal application build uses the committed offline guide resources. Prettier Standalone and sql-formatter are copied as compact browser bundles and execute offline in JavaFX WebView without Node.
Packaging is pinned to the JDK 25 toolchain

The packaged runtime explicitly includes KTPH000, which JavaFX WebView needs and which was removed in JDK 26. The removal is tracked as OpenJDK issue KTPH001: KTPH006https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8362628KTPH007. Every packaging task resolves KTPH002 from the same Gradle-selected Temurin JDK 25 toolchain as compilation, so a newer system KTPH003 or KTPH004 cannot silently create an incompatible runtime. The selected toolchain must still match the target CPU because KTPH005 does not cross-compile.

Verify the host tools and inspect the JDKs Gradle can select before the first build. The system JDK may be newer than 25, but KTPH000 must list a matching JDK 25 for the target CPU after provisioning; Maven must use a JDK that can build SithTermFX.

The first wrapper invocation downloads Gradle. A clean application build also clones SithTermFX when necessary, installs it through Maven, downloads the pinned build inputs, compiles korTTY and runs the tests.

KTPH000 assembles KTPH001 with one final Gradle KTPH002. It removes stale dependency versions and formatter trees, keeps only the current mosh4j architecture and protobuf, reuses the application's parent-loaded Bouncy Castle, excludes SithTermFX's test dependency, and replaces JNA/pty4j with JARs that retain all Java classes, services, manifests and licences but only the target native path and binary architecture. The verification task deliberately seeds obsolete files before Sync and runs a real JNA/PTY smoke against the slim JARs:

The platform-independent size reporter separates the app image, runtime, formatter/Mosh payloads, dependency JARs and compressed application-JAR resources, then writes JSON and Markdown. It understands the macOS KTPH000 and KTPH001, Windows KTPH002 and KTPH003, and Linux KTPH004 and KTPH005 layouts produced by KTPH006. CI compares native installers with the committed release baseline, requires at least 15% reduction, applies the 180 MiB app-image and 145 MiB DMG limits, and uses a 2% regression tolerance once a new platform size is verified:

Before a Windows archive is created, the release workflow resolves the generated app image and requires an application JAR, KTPH000, at least 100 MiB of plausible content and x86_64 PE headers for both launcher and JVM. Linux RPM size enforcement runs after KTPH001, so the measured file is the one that is distributed.
Use the platform command below to compile, test and create the thin JAR plus the Java ZIP and TAR distributions:

The thin JAR contains korTTY classes and resources but not its runtime dependencies and does not provide the complete deployment by itself. For a Java-based portable layout, extract the generated ZIP or TAR and start KTPH000 on macOS/Linux or KTPH001 on Windows; the destination still needs JDK 25. These distributions also contain the native JavaFX dependencies selected on the build host, so build them on the same OS and architecture on which they will run.
Build a separate llama.cpp runtime packageKTPH000

Integrated local AI uses a native artifact that is intentionally separate from every KTPH000 app image and installer. KTPH001 is the single build contract for its upstream tag, full commit, source-archive SHA-256, korTTY runtime revision, and API-contract version. KTPH002 fails closed when those values or the requested backend are invalid.

Install CMake and a native C/C++ toolchain. A Vulkan package additionally needs the Vulkan headers, loader, and shader compiler; Metal is available only on macOS with the Apple development tools. Then build the package for the current machine:

The task chain downloads only the pinned commit archive, verifies its SHA-256, extracts it, configures a Release build with curl, RPC, tests, examples, tools, and server Web UI disabled, builds KTPH000, stages its required libraries and license, and creates a reproducible ZIP plus JSON descriptor under KTPH001. The descriptor records the immutable runtime ID, tag/commit, API-contract version, minimum korTTY version, platform, architecture, concrete backend, package size/SHA-256, publication URL placeholder, entrypoint, and revocation flag.
One build host cannot create the whole matrix

Native llama.cpp artifacts follow the same target-platform rule as KTPH000: build each operating-system/architecture/backend combination on a matching host. The runtime workflow covers macOS arm64/x86_64 CPU+Metal, Windows x86_64 CPU+Vulkan, Linux x86_64/arm64 CPU+Vulkan. CUDA is not in the first matrix.
Candidate detection, contract tests, and promotionKTPH000

KTPH000 checks upstream tags daily. A change opens a candidate PR that updates the source pin but does not publish it. Pull requests and manual builds run the native matrix; every artifact must start and report its version, the Linux CPU reference job additionally verifies unauthenticated rejection, authenticated model listing, completion, sleep/wake, JSON-schema chat completion, embeddings, and two simultaneously usable sidecars, and a pinned Qdrant 1.18.2 service runs the real vector-store contract. The korTTY repository owns only candidate detection and source-side matrix validation: it has no stable-promotion action, cross-repository release token, or runtime signing private key.

Stable publication belongs to the public KTPH003chardonnay/kortty-llama-runtimesKTPH004 repository. Its explicit human-dispatched workflow accepts the exact reviewed korTTY source commit, rebuilds the native matrix, runs authentication, chat/completion, embeddings, JSON-schema, sleep/wake, and parallel-sidecar smoke tests on every package, and runs the pinned Qdrant contract separately. After those checks it enters the protected KTPH000 environment, verifies that KTPH001 matches the published trust root, verifies and extends the cumulative signed index, and creates an immutable runtime-only release with that repository's scoped KTPH002; no cross-repository personal access token is required. An existing runtime ID is never overwritten. Regular promotion is limited to once every seven days, while an audited security or model-support reason can override that cadence. The application installer therefore stays unchanged while a compatible native runtime can be promoted or withdrawn independently.
Publish the model and prompt catalogKTPH000

The reviewed canonical catalog is KTPH000. It uses strict schema v1 for local-model recommendations and model-name-to-preset mappings; application code and prompt-contract text are not part of this independently released payload.

KTPH000 is manual-only, accepts dispatches only from KTPH001, and has no preview or automatic promotion path. Its dispatch requires the exact reviewed KTPH002 and a release repository, defaulting to KTPH003. Before signing, it verifies that the positive catalog sequence is strictly greater than the latest published sequence and runs the authoritative Java schema/trust-chain tests. The KTPH004 GitHub environment must have required reviewers before production secrets are configured; inside it, the workflow checks that KTPH005 matches the Ed25519 private signing secret, signs the unchanged JSON bytes, verifies the signature, and publishes immutable KTPH006 plus KTPH007. An existing version tag or release is refused. Configure KTPH008 and KTPH009 only as environment-scoped promotion secrets.

Every application release that may install runtimes or refresh the catalog must embed both Ed25519 KTPH001publicKTPH002 verification keys. The runtime-channel trust root is public, auditable, and pinned in KTPH000, so normal local builds use the same key as official packages. The catalog trust root is supplied separately. Never provide either signing private key to an application build.
Optional KTPH000; must match the pinned key exactly
Optional KTPH000; must match the pinned key exactly
The generated resources store the fixed channel URLs and public trust roots with the application:

The official application-release workflow reads both names from GitHub Actions repository variables, rejects missing values or private-key material, and lets Gradle validate the X.509 Ed25519 keys before packaging. The runtime variable is a redundant CI identity check and must encode the same public key as the tracked PEM; a different override fails the build instead of replacing the trust root. If the pinned runtime key or generated release configuration is missing or malformed, runtime installation/update fails closed before fetching the index. Without the catalog key, korTTY makes no catalog request, ignores any cache, and uses its built-in bootstrap.

Install the common prerequisites and Apple command-line tooling. The unsigned KTPH000 build uses the JDK tools; DMG creation uses KTPH001 and the configured custom icon, while signing and notarization additionally use KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004 and KTPH005. Select a current Xcode installation before a release build.

Run KTPH000 if the command-line tools are absent. A release intended for other users also needs an Apple Developer account, a KTPH001Developer ID ApplicationKTPH002 certificate and App Store Connect API credentials for notarization; an unsigned local build does not.
Build an unsigned app image, portable ZIP and DMGKTPH000
Open the app image for a local smoke test and verify the DMG container:

The reliable paths are an Intel Mac with an x86_64 JDK 25 or the repository's GitHub Actions job on KTPH000. KTPH001 does not cross-compile, so an ARM JDK running natively on Apple Silicon creates an ARM app even if the desired filename says KTPH002.
On an Intel Mac, validate the machine, Java runtime and generated launcher before distributing the result:
The final KTPH000 command must print only KTPH001. Perform the same build on Apple Silicon with an ARM JDK to obtain the separate KTPH002 artifacts; the project does not create a universal binary.

The KTPH000 workflow contains separate macOS matrix entries for KTPH001/KTPH002 and KTPH003/KTPH004. It installs Temurin JDK 25, rejects a JDK or runner architecture mismatch, builds both the signed app and DMG, verifies the launcher with KTPH005, notarizes both deliverables and uploads architecture-suffixed artifacts.
Configure these repository secrets before running the workflow:
Base64-encoded Developer ID Application certificate and private key in P12 form
Exact Developer ID Application identity shown by KTPH000
App Store Connect API key ID

Open KTPH004Actions → Build Release Binaries → Run workflowKTPH005, choose the branch or tag in KTPH000, and enter its numeric application version. A branch run uploads the macOS build artifacts for inspection; a published GitHub Release, or a manual run whose KTPH001 is a release tag, also feeds the final release-upload job. The Intel artifacts are named KTPH002 and KTPH003.
Rosetta is an unverified advanced path

An Apple Silicon host can experimentally run an x86_64 JDK 25 under Rosetta, but this is not the repository's verified release path. Install Rosetta, select an Intel JDK for both KTPH000 and KTPH001, stop existing Gradle daemons, run the complete build in an x86_64 shell and confirm the launcher with KTPH002. Test the result on real Intel hardware before distribution; use KTPH003 when a reproducible release artifact is required.

Signing is opt-in. The Gradle tasks use the repository properties below to sign bundled JNA/pty4j native libraries and pass the identity to KTPH000; do not replace this flow with an ad-hoc signature over only the outer app bundle.

If the identity is stored in a non-default keychain, add KTPH000 to both packaging commands. Signing and notarization are separate operations: the Gradle properties sign the artifacts but do not submit them to Apple's notary service.

The release workflow is the canonical automated implementation. To mirror its notarization phase locally, store the App Store Connect API credentials in a keychain profile, submit a ZIP of the signed KTPH000, staple the accepted ticket, then submit and staple the signed DMG.
Inspect any rejected submission with KTPH000. Before publishing, verify Gatekeeper, the embedded signatures, the stapled tickets and the launcher architecture:
KTPH000 reports a signing identity error: run KTPH001, copy the complete Developer ID Application identity and confirm that the selected keychain is unlocked.
KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002 or the generated launcher report different architectures: install a matching JDK, update KTPH003 and KTPH004, run KTPH005, then rebuild from KTPH006.

Notarization fails: read the submission log instead of re-signing individual JavaFX libraries; the repository deliberately preserves their upstream signatures while separately signing the native libraries covered by its Gradle task.
The packaged app can reach a LAN host but KTPH000 cannot: launch the KTPH001 so macOS can grant Local Network permission to the application bundle.
KTPH000Apple: Signing Mac software with Developer IDKTPH001
KTPH000Apple: Notarizing macOS software before distributionKTPH001

The app-image task needs the common prerequisites. DEB creation needs KTPH000; RPM creation needs the RPM build tools; KTPH001 is needed only when you want the portable ZIP in addition to the TAR.GZ archive.

Install and select the full JDK 25 separately if the distribution command does not provide that exact JDK. Build DEB packages on Debian/Ubuntu and RPM packages on an RPM-based distribution; the portable app image is available on either family.
Build the app image, portable archives and packagesKTPH000
Then create the native package for the current distribution:
Run and inspect the outputs without installing the packages:

Use only the inspection command available for the package you built. Test installer installation and removal in a disposable virtual machine or container matching the target distribution before publishing it.
KTPH000 fails with a missing KTPH001: install KTPH002 and rerun from a clean build directory.
KTPH000 cannot find KTPH001: install KTPH002 on RPM distributions or KTPH003 on Debian/Ubuntu, then confirm KTPH004.
The KTPH000 task succeeds but no KTPH001 appears: this is expected; inspect KTPH002, which is the self-contained jpackage app-image directory.
KTPH000 reports that the destination already exists: run KTPH001 before rebuilding the app image.
KTPH000Debian Handbook: inspecting packages with dpkgKTPH001

Use a PowerShell terminal with the common prerequisites. The portable app-image task needs no external installer builder, but MSI creation requires WiX Toolset 3 or later with KTPH000 and KTPH001 available in KTPH002. The release workflow uses the WiX 3 toolchain for its Windows packaging jobs.
Restart PowerShell after changing KTPH000, KTPH001 or the WiX installation so the wrapper and KTPH002 see the new values.
Build the app image, portable ZIP and MSIKTPH000
Windows launcher inside the app image
The ZIP is portable because it contains the complete KTPH000 directory. KTPH001 is a launcher within that directory, not a stand-alone binary; extract the entire directory before running it.

The release workflow currently publishes the validated x86_64 Windows package only. OpenJFX does not provide native Windows ARM artifacts for the pinned JavaFX line, so Windows-on-ARM uses this x86_64 package through Windows emulation; the former mislabeled ARM archive is no longer produced or used as a size baseline. Native Windows ARM packaging requires a separate JavaFX/JDK packaging track and native WebView/PTY validation.
Test MSI installation, launch, upgrade and removal in a disposable Windows virtual machine matching the target architecture before publishing it.
KTPH000 reports that WiX cannot be found: confirm that KTPH001 succeeds in the same PowerShell session, then rerun KTPH002 and KTPH003.
Gradle cannot resolve the packaging JDK: run KTPH000, allow toolchain downloads or install a native JDK 25, then stop existing daemons with KTPH001.
Maven cannot build SithTermFX: confirm that KTPH000 reports JDK 25 and that KTPH001 is available in KTPH002.
The app-image destination already exists: run KTPH000 before rebuilding.
A packaging task for another operating system is absent: this is expected because KTPH000 registers KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003 and KTPH004 only on their matching host platforms.

A clean build cannot resolve dependencies or download a pinned asset: confirm outbound HTTPS access and proxy configuration for GitHub, Maven repositories, Gradle services, Node.js and the npm registry, then rerun the failed Gradle task.
Gradle uses a different Java runtime after KTPH000 changes: stop the daemon with KTPH001 or KTPH002, verify KTPH003, and rebuild from KTPH004.
A package has the wrong architecture: compare the OS architecture with the KTPH000 line from KTPH001; install a native JDK 25 matching the target and rebuild rather than renaming the output.
